tier_reason: docs/tinydrivers/getting-started.mdx (Performance section) gives a first-party '~40ms faster' figure on 620 queries against QtSql/QMYSQL, measured once on a GCC 13.2.1 Debug build with no CPU model and no total runtime; a Debug build caps the tier at C. The workload program (silverqx/TinyOrmPlayground) is public but has no timing harness or published results.

corrections.caveats: Weak claim: first-party, one run, Debug build (tier capped at C), no CPU model, no run-to-run variance, no total elapsed time (so no ratio can be derived), and the author concludes the two are 'very similar' because 90% of the time is spent inside the MySQL C API. The speed-up is about 40 ms on 620 queries (roughly 65 microseconds per query, tuned with KCacheGrind) and is driver overhead, not database work. The README's other claim ('1000 complex queries in 500ms, heavily DB dependent, the PostgreSQL is by far the fastest') has no baseline. The benchmark program, silverqx/TinyOrmPlayground (public, MIT, 0 stars, 444 commits), has build manifests for both TinyDrivers and QtSql but no timing harness or results in its README, so the 40 ms cannot be reproduced from published material. Category 'database-client-drivers' is outside the six wave-6 categories; the seed line guessed embedded-kv. Last commit 2024-08-26 (commits/main page); the repo shows 5,739 commits.

notes: Claim matches the Performance section of getting-started.mdx word for word; tier C stands; metadata confirmed (MIT, 353 stars, 37 forks, last commit 2024-08-26, stale). Shortcomings to record: effectively parity with QtSql/QMYSQL by the author's own conclusion (~40 ms over 620 queries, no total time), single first-party Debug-build run with no CPU model, workload program public but without a timing harness, and category database-client-drivers is not a wave-6 category (orchestrator must file it, e.g. by category override).

tier_reason: The MySQL column in pgtpc sysbench/ref-mysql.md is copied from Oracle's own MySQL performance blog posts (vendor numbers, different machine, CPU model not stated), while the PostgreSQL column comes from public sysbench commands and config in sysbench/aws.c5d.metal.extreme.md on an AWS c5d.metal with no CPU model; a cross-machine, vendor-sourced comparison is C at best.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Queries per second as tabulated in pgtpc sysbench/ref-mysql.md: oltp_read_write MySQL.48C 900,000 vs PGSQL.48C 722,907 (1.25x, derived from page data), the only MySQL-favourable row; the PGSQL.96C column gives 910,554, which the raw log in aws.c5d.metal.extreme.md records at thread = 128 (parity). PostgreSQL is ahead or level on every other row: oltp_point_select 1,050,000 vs 1,814,404 (the PGSQL.48C figure equals the page's own c=64 raw-data row; its c=48 row is 1,503,656, still 1.43x ahead, derived from page data) and 2,332,928 at c=104; oltp_read_only 920,000 vs 941,694; oltp_update_non_index 240,000 vs 269,233. The pgtpc README summary: 'PGSQL has a similar write performance and significantly better read performance to MySQL.'
corrections.workload: sysbench on 8 tables (10M rows each for oltp_read_only, oltp_read_write and oltp_update_non_index; 50M rows each for oltp_point_select). MySQL 8.0 'extreme config' (checksum, doublewrite, binlog, performance schema and fsync off, latin1) from Oracle's published runs on a 48-core 2.7 GHz box with 2x Optane P4800X, versus PostgreSQL (14.5 per the same machine's normal-config page) with fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off, wal_level minimal, LATIN1 and prewarmed tables, run by the pgtpc author on AWS c5d.metal with threads forced to 48 (read_write also at 128, point_select swept 1-512).
corrections.license: GPL-2.0-only (with Oracle's additional linking permission; libmysqlclient also under the Universal FOSS Exception 1.0)

notes: All tabulated numbers match ref-mysql.md and the PostgreSQL raw log; corrections fix the '96 threads' label (the 910,554 read_write run was at 128 threads), note that the 48C point-select figure is really the c=64 row, and point benchmark_url at the comparison page. Shortcomings to record: not faster than PostgreSQL (wins only oltp_read_write at 48 threads, by 1.25x, against a run on a different machine; loses point_select by 1.4-1.7x; parity or behind elsewhere), MySQL numbers are vendor-published (Oracle's MySQL performance blog at dimitrik.free.fr, unreachable here: ENOTFOUND) on different hardware with no CPU model, durability-off configs on both sides, wrong category (client-server RDBMS filed as embedded-kv), and the wave-6 postgres/postgres record uses the same pgtpc page in the opposite direction.

tier_reason: First-party blog numbers (ODB's author) seen only through search-result snippets because codesynthesis.com is unreachable (ENOTFOUND); the snippets confirm ODB 24 ms vs 47 ms hand-coded C# and 49 ms Dapper per 500 iterations, but no benchmark code, compiler or flags were found, and the C# side is Dapper's own figures on unstated hardware with SQL Server. Snippet-only evidence is capped at C.

corrections.hardware: ODB side: Intel Xeon E5520 at 2.27 GHz (snippet only). C#/Dapper side: not stated by Dapper (snippet only).
corrections.license: GPL-2.0-only or commercial (libodb, libodb-sqlite, libodb-pgsql, libodb-mysql, libodb-qt, libodb-boost); GPL-3.0-only (odb compiler); NCUEL non-commercial or commercial (libodb-oracle, libodb-mssql); Unlicense (odb-example)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 65 stars, 6 forks, 5,139 commits on GitHub; long-standing C++ ORM with MySQL, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server backends
corrections.caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: codesynthesis.com is unreachable from this session (DNS ENOTFOUND for WebFetch), so the 2011-04-06 blog post and the January 2012 follow-up were never opened; the figures come from WebSearch result summaries, which also say the ODB run used a Xeon E5520 2.27 GHz machine while Dapper's numbers name no hardware. The C# figures (47 ms hand-coded SqlDataReader, 49 ms Dapper) are Dapper's published numbers on a different machine, a different database (SQL Server) and a different language, so the roughly 2x is indicative only. Roughly 15-year-old numbers on MySQL 5.1, PostgreSQL 9.0 and SQLite 3.7; the exact database versions were not re-confirmed in the snippets seen. No benchmark source, compiler or flags were found. The repo carries no benchmark claims, and no comparison against another C++ ORM (sqlpp11, SOCI, sqlite_orm, Wt::Dbo) was found. Licensing is split per package: runtime libraries GPL-2.0-only or commercial, compiler GPL-3.0-only, but the Oracle and SQL Server runtimes are under the non-OSI NCUEL, hence usability mixed. Category embedded-kv does not fit an ORM.

notes: Blog post blocked (ENOTFOUND), but two WebSearch snippets corroborate 24 ms vs 47 ms/49 ms per 500 iterations and the PostgreSQL 27 ms / MySQL 24 ms / SQLite 7 ms follow-up; tier C kept on snippet-only evidence; usability corrected to mixed because libodb-oracle and libodb-mssql are NCUEL. Shortcomings to record: snippet-only first-party evidence, cross-language, cross-database (MySQL vs SQL Server) and cross-machine comparison against Dapper's own figures, 2011-era versions, no benchmark code or flags, off-category (ORM filed under embedded-kv).
